statement: An integral is the continuous analog of a sum, used to calculate areas, volumes, and their generalizations. For a real-valued function f on a closed interval [a, b] with a < b, the definite integral \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx computes the signed area of the region bounded by the graph of f between a and b, defined by evaluating upper and lower sums on a partition a = x_0 \le x_1 \le \dots \le x_n = b, with conventions \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = -\int_{b}^{a} f(x)\,dx for a > b and \int_{a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0.

symbols.meaning: definite integral of f over [a, b]

properties.why: integration is a linear functional on the vector space of integrable functions
defines integration when the upper limit is strictly less than the lower limit
an integral taken over a degenerate interval or single point is zero
integrability on an interval implies integrability on subintervals and additivity across an intermediate point

properties.property: m(b - a) \le \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx \le M(b - a) \text{ for } m \le f(x) \le M
properties.why: upper and lower sums of f over [a, b] are bounded by m(b - a) and M(b - a)
upper and lower sums of f are bounded above by the respective sums of g
Riemann integrability of f implies Riemann integrability of |f|
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality holds for Riemann-integrable functions
first fundamental theorem of calculus establishes differentiation and integration as inverse operations for continuous functions

properties.property: \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) \text{ where } F'(x) = f(x)
properties.why: second fundamental theorem of calculus computes definite integrals from antiderivatives

assumptions.assumption: The integrand f is bounded on [a, b]
assumptions.breaks_when: The function f has an infinite singularity in [a, b], requiring an improper integral

assumptions.assumption: The domain [a, b] is a closed and bounded interval
assumptions.breaks_when: The interval is unbounded (e.g. extending to infinity), requiring an improper integral defined by limits

failure_modes.mode: Improper integral due to unbounded domain
failure_modes.cause: Proper Riemann integral assumes a finite closed interval; must be evaluated as \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_a^b f(x)\,dx, which may not converge

failure_modes.mode: Improper integral due to unbounded integrand
failure_modes.signature: Integrand f(x) diverges or is undefined at an endpoint or interior point
failure_modes.cause: Proper Riemann integral requires f to be finite and defined on [a, b]; must be evaluated via a limit such as \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} \int_{a+\epsilon}^b f(x)\,dx, which may diverge
